opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so a lot of it came from watching what our own customers were actually doing. When we first started talking to teams about agents, there was this assumption that coding agents were one category, the thing that helps your engineers write software, and then "custom agents" were a separate category, the thing you build to automate some business process like triaging support tickets or answering questions over your data. People thought of them as different products with different buyers.

But when you look under the hood, the hard problems are almost identical. In both cases you have a model that needs to take actions over a bunch of steps, call tools, read and write data, and you need to know whether it's doing the right thing. You need governance: what is this agent allowed to touch? You need evaluation: how do I know version two is better than version one? You need tracing and observability when something goes wrong. And you need it all connected to the data, because whether the agent is writing a SQL pipeline or answering a customer question, the quality comes down to whether it understands your data and your context.

The other thing we noticed is that the line between the two is blurring really fast. A lot of the most useful "custom" agents are basically coding agents underneath. They write a query, run some code, look at the result, and iterate. And on the flip side, coding agents increasingly need enterprise context, like which tables are trustworthy, what the business definitions are, and who has access to what. So if you build two separate stacks, you end up duplicating permissions, duplicating evaluation infrastructure, and duplicating all the plumbing, and the two drift apart.

So our view was that the platform should treat an agent as an agent. Give it the same access controls, the same eval and monitoring tooling, and the same connection to the data layer, and then let people specialize it for coding or for a specific business task on top of that. That also means improvements compound. If we make the tracing better or the evaluation better for one use case, everyone benefits.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it came from watching what people actually did with coding agents once they had them. We built the coding agent first because software engineering is the domain where you have the best feedback loops: you can run tests, you can compile, you can lint, you can diff. The agent gets a signal about whether it did the right thing without a human in the loop every step. So that's where the agent loop matured fastest, and that's where the tooling, the sandboxing, the file system access, the permission model, all of that got hardened.

But then you look at what users were building, and a huge fraction of it wasn't really "coding" in the sense of shipping a pull request. People were using the coding agent to do data analysis, to generate reports, to wire up API calls, to orchestrate other scripts. They were essentially building custom agents by abusing the coding agent, because it was the one that had a good harness. And when we looked at the architecture, there's no real reason the harness should be special-cased to code. An agent is a loop: a model, a set of tools, some state, and a policy for when to ask the human. Whether the tools are a bash shell and a file editor, or a SQL warehouse and a ticketing system, the loop is the same.

The other thing is that the things that make a coding agent good are exactly the things enterprises want in any agent. They want observability, so they can see every tool call. They want governance, so they can say "this agent can read these tables but not those." They want evals, so they can tell if a change to the prompt or the model made things worse. If you build two separate platforms, you end up re-implementing all of that twice, and the custom-agent platform is always the one that lags, because the coding agent has a more vocal user base.

So the bet is: make the coding agent one instance of a general agent runtime, and let the people who are building custom agents get the same quality bar for free. In practice I think it also goes the other direction. Once your custom agent can call the coding agent as a tool, you get agents that can extend themselves. The data agent that hits a gap can write the connector it needs. That's hard to do if they're living in different worlds.

astra-6.text:
The connection is that coding is often one part of a much broader task. A coding agent needs to find information, use tools, test what it did, and adjust based on the result. A custom agent doing data analysis or helping with a business workflow needs many of those same capabilities. And it may benefit from writing code along the way, even if you wouldn’t describe it as a coding agent.

So it seemed natural to share the underlying platform—the tool access, the execution environment, the permissions, and the ability to evaluate whether the agent actually accomplished the task. You can specialize the experience for different users, but you don’t necessarily want to build that infrastructure twice.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that coding is a capability almost any useful agent will need. Even if you’re building an agent to do research or analyze business data, it may want to write a SQL query, run some Python, or build a small tool to answer a question. So the distinction between a coding agent and a custom agent starts to blur.

And they need a lot of the same infrastructure: a secure environment to execute code, access to tools and data, permission controls, and a way to evaluate whether they’re doing the right thing. It seemed natural to build those capabilities on a shared platform, so a custom agent can use code whenever that’s the best way to accomplish its task.
